items.title: Wellman Braud Interview, 1958-03-31
items.q: I had a friend of mine by the name of Wilbur Sweatman

ctx.x: Did they ever use banjos when you were down here much?

No, guitar. Only after I left here, when banjos got popular, I think around 1917 or 18, because all the bands up north were using banjos. Did they use tubas in the band? And I had a friend of mine by the name of Wilbur Sweatman, I guess you heard that. He wrote the Down Home Rag. Where...
This is not that master, it's a different one. This is the Bluebird I got here.

items.title: Wellman Braud Interview, 1958-03-31
items.q: But after a while, you can sit in the orchestra, and, well, I don't know, I sit just on, besides Elgar's band, that's the only big orchestra. And when I played with Elgar, there wasn't no arrangement

ctx.x: One time Barney told me something about how you all took the tune, that was one of Oliver's numbers, I think, in the Camp Meeting Blues. And you were part of that bar, the Creole Love.

Yeah, Creole Love called, and we also, high number we had written by Lorenzo Teal, Mood Enigo. Oh, was that really? Oh, yeah, that was really. But you see, the Ellington is a doctor of music, I'll call him, because he can make a tune a little better and sound a little better than what it is. It'll come from his brain, it still comes from the same thing of improvising. Now, I see in places, I take an eighth note, if it's on the score, and I can make a thirty-second note out of it, but I know where to put it at.…
In the old days, before you, when you were just a kid and heard the first bass players, how many beats in a major did they play? Did they play something like that? Two beats.
